raw_case_text:
A 48-year-old woman came to the surgical outpatient unit complaining of painless swelling on the left anterior chest wall below the medial end of the clavicle for 45 days. She gave history of an increase in swelling size, pain, and difficulty in swallowing for 15 days. She is a known case of Sjogren syndrome and hypothyroidism. She had no history of fever, cough, or loss of appetite. No significant family history was present. On physical examination, the swelling was 3 cm x 3 cm, and the overlying skin and temperature were normal [Figure 1a arrow]. She had no history of trauma. A clinical diagnosis of a cold abscess was suspected.
Initial laboratory investigations revealed hemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 80 mm and C-reactive protein of 37 mg/L. Serology for human immunodeficiency virus was negative. She was mildly anemic.
Ultrasonography (USG) of swelling revealed a well-defined heterogeneous hypoechoic lesion measuring 2.7 cm x 2.8 cm in the subcutaneous plane on the left side below medial end of the clavicle. Bone destruction was noted at the anterior cortex of the clavicle, with surrounding fat inflamed and hyperechoic. A diagnosis of early abscess was suggested. X-ray chest revealed focal cortical destruction in the left side of the sternum. No obvious opacities were seen in both lungs [Figure 1b arrow].
High resolution computed tomography (HRCT) thorax and abdomen scans showed focal bone destruction with the erosion of the anterior cortex on the left side of the manubrium sternum and the anterior cortex of the medial end of left clavicle. A well-defined hypodense collection with peripheral rim enhancement was noted in the subcutaneous region of the anterior chest wall. It was located anterior to the manubrium sternum on the left side, extending into the left sternoclavicular joint with the destruction of the anterior wall of clavicle [Figure 1c and d arrow]. Heterogeneously enhancing nonnecrotic left axillary and anterior chest wall lymph nodes were noted. No obvious enhancing lesions were seen in bilateral lungs, pleura, and other organs. A diagnosis of abscess with underlying osteomyelitis was suggested.
USG-guided aspiration was done from the swelling with aseptic precautions. Yellow white material was aspirated. Out of three smears, two smears were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) and one smear was stained with Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) stain. The remaining material was sent for molecular studies. H and E stained smears showed amorphous to granular eosinophilic material (caseous necrosis) with many viable polymorphs, red blood cells, and lymphocytes [Figure 2a arrow]. ZN stain showed many acid-fast bacilli [Figure 2b arrow]. A diagnosis of tubercular abscess was made.
Cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and susceptible to rifampicin. Culture for acid-fast bacteria (AFB) was positive. The diagnosis of TB was confirmed. Sputum for AFB was negative. Intensive anti-tubercular regime of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol was started for 2 months and will be followed by maintenance therapy for 6-9 months depending on clinical response. The patient is on treatment for 2 months, and swelling appears to be slightly reduced clinically.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 48-year-old woman presented with a 45-day history of a left upper anterior chest wall swelling below the medial clavicle that became painful and enlarged over the past 15 days with dysphagia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient noticed a painless left infraclavicular/parasternal swelling 45 days prior to presentation, which increased in size over the last 15 days and became associated with local pain and difficulty swallowing.
subjective.past_medical_history: Known history of Sjögren syndrome and hypothyroidism; no history of trauma or family history of TB.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for local chest wall pain and dysphagia; negative for fever, cough, or loss of appetite.

objective.physical_examination: A 3 cm × 3 cm swelling on the left anterior chest wall inferior to the medial end of the left clavicle with normal overlying skin and local temperature.
objective.routine_investigations: Hb 9.8 g/dL (mild anemia), ESR 80 mm/h, CRP 37 mg/L, HIV serology negative, sputum AFB smear negative. Chest X-ray showed focal cortical bone destruction on the left side of the sternum with clear lung fields. High-resolution ultrasound showed a 2.7 × 2.8 cm well-defined heterogeneous hypoechoic subcutaneous collection below the medial left clavicle with anterior clavicular cortical destruction and surrounding fat inflammation.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic and abdominal HRCT demonstrated focal cortical erosion of the left manubrium sterni and medial left clavicle with a rim-enhancing hypodense subcutaneous collection extending into the left sternoclavicular joint, accompanied by heterogeneously enhancing non-necrotic left axillary and anterior chest wall lymph nodes and normal lungs/pleura. Ultrasound-guided aspiration yielded yellow-white pus showing caseous necrosis with polymorphs and lymphocytes on H&E stain.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Aspirated pus from the left sternoclavicular abscess was positive for numerous acid-fast bacilli on Ziehl-Neelsen stain, positive for rifampicin-susceptible Mycobacterium tuberculosis on CBNAAT, and positive on AFB culture, confirming primary tuberculous sternoclavicular osteomyelitis with a cold abscess. She was started on a 2-month intensive phase of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (to be followed by 6–9 months of maintenance therapy), showing clinical reduction of the swelling at 2-month follow-up.
